business: Parity (free, open-source behavior proof for software changes)
by_segment: Owner or office manager of a small business running an old Windows app
Developer in a product team that uses AI coding agents daily
Consultant at an IT services firm doing legacy migrations
IT staff in a public body (city, hospital, school district)
Solo developer or freelancer maintaining client apps
why_not: This is exactly my problem on legacy migrations, but I can't put an unknown tool on a client's app this month. Security would ask what gets sent to Meta's models and whether recordings of client screens leave the machine, and I have no answer to show them.

I do need something like this, since I'm merging AI-written changes into an old app I can't fully check myself. But I can't take a free student project to my manager and security people and ask them to let it record screens of our business app and send them to Meta's AI.

I'm not rewriting my old app this month, and if I ever do, whoever I pay to migrate it should be the one proving it works. Recording, sandboxing and confirming a list of business rules on my own machine is way more than an hour I don't have.

Free is nice, but I don't have an afternoon to install a local tool, set up a sandbox, record every workflow and then check a list of business rules some AI wrote. I just eyeball the agent's PRs, run what tests we have, and move on.

Our unit and end-to-end tests in CI already catch what the agent breaks in the PRs I merge, so I don't have a painful gap this would fill. Recording sessions and then reviewing a list of business rules an AI guessed sounds like a second test suite I'd have to babysit.

I already have unit tests, end-to-end tests and CI catching regressions, and recording scenarios then checking AI-written business rules sounds like a second test suite to babysit. Free doesn't help much when the real cost is my time in the middle of a migration I've already put off for a year.
why_yes: It's free, it runs locally, and I'm merging AI-written PRs every week, so I'll clone it and try it once on the old Windows app. My tests cover the code I know about. They don't cover the business rules nobody ever wrote down.

It's free and runs locally, and I'm merging agent-written PRs I don't fully read, so I'd clone it and try it once on a side project. Whether it stays installed depends on the first run, not the pitch.
flip: A published case study or a reproducible demo on a messy real-world legacy app, plus a clear statement that capture can run on local models with nothing leaving the machine, so I can get it past our security review.

Watching it catch a real regression on one of our own apps in under an hour of setup, fully offline, with no data leaving the box.
